facts.text: It is one of the smallest of all Australian birds, measuring just 8 to 10 centimetres long.
facts.quote: One of the smallest of all Australian birds at 8 to 10 centimetres (3.1 to 3.9 in) in length

facts.text: The adult male has grey-brown upperparts with buff spots, a black crown, white-spotted wings and tail, and a reddish rump.
facts.quote: The adult male of the nominate subspecies has grey-brown upperparts with numerous paler buff spots, a black crown, wings and tail all with white spots, white eyebrows and reddish rump.

facts.text: Pairs exchange soft, whistling wheet-wheet calls throughout the day that carry a long way.
facts.quote: Pairs make soft, whistling wheet-wheet calls to one another throughout the day, which carry for quite a distance.

facts.text: Its contact call is really two calls—an initial call and an almost instant reply—so it can seem to come from two directions at once.
facts.quote: the contact call is in fact two calls: an initial call and an almost instant response, and thus can come from two different directions.

facts.text: It nests underground, digging a tunnel up to 1.5 metres long to a chamber lined with shredded bark.
facts.quote: The nest is an underground horizontal oval chamber lined with shredded bark, linked by a tunnel 0.5 to 1.5 metres (1 ft 8 in to 4 ft 11 in) long to a hole in the side of a riverbank or slope in a shaded location.

facts.text: Some pardalotes have taken to nesting in carpet rolls and garage roll-a-doors.
facts.quote: Birds have used carpet rolls and garage roll-a-doors to nest in on occasion.

facts.text: The female lays 3 to 4 shiny white eggs, which hatch after 19 days of incubation.
facts.quote: producing a clutch of 3 to 4 round shiny white eggs 16 mm (0.63 in) long by 13 mm (0.51 in) wide. The eggs are incubated for 19 days until they hatch

facts.text: Although moderately common across fertile parts of Australia, it is seldom seen closely enough to identify.
facts.quote: Although moderately common in all of the reasonably fertile parts of Australia (the east coast, the south-east, and the south-west corner) it is seldom seen closely enough to enable identification.

facts.text: Numbers appear to be declining, especially in urban areas, but the species is not considered endangered.
facts.quote: Spotted pardalote numbers appear to be declining, especially in urban areas, but the species is not considered endangered at this time.
